summary:
Project Description – Flame in Freefall

Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data is a research-support platform designed to explore how fire behaves in microgravity environments, particularly in spacecraft.

The project uses data from NASA combustion experiments to analyse flame behaviour under microgravity conditions. It aims to identify patterns and relationships between factors such as flame temperature, flame size, fuel type, oxygen concentration, and combustion duration, depending on the available dataset.

Our platform combines data analysis, interactive visualisations, and machine learning techniques to help users understand changes in combustion behaviour and explore potential fire hazards in space environments.

It addresses the challenge by transforming complex scientific data into understandable insights that can support research into spacecraft fire safety. By making combustion data easier to explore and interpret, the project aims to contribute to better understanding of fire behaviour and future fire-prevention research for space missions.

Team: LLOXELL
details:
1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

Flame in Freefall is a research-support platform that explores how flames behave in microgravity. It analyses combustion data from space-based experiments to understand changes in flame temperature, flame size, fuel behaviour and other available parameters. The platform uses data processing, visualisations and machine learning techniques to identify patterns and present scientific insights in an understandable way.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Makes complex combustion data easier to understand.
  • Helps researchers explore flame behaviour in microgravity.
  • Identifies patterns that may support future fire-safety research.
  • Provides interactive visualisations for analysing experimental data.
  • Encourages the use of AI and data science in space research.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our intended impact is to support research into safer space environments by improving our understanding of fire behaviour in microgravity. The project aims to make NASA combustion data more accessible and useful for students, researchers and space-science enthusiasts. It is a research-support concept, not a certified spacecraft fire-safety system.

4. What tools did you use?

  • Python: Data processing and analysis.
  • Pandas and NumPy: Data handling and numerical calculations.
  • Scikit-learn: Machine learning and pattern analysis.
  • React and Vite: Frontend development.
  • Tailwind CSS: User interface design.
  • FastAPI: Backend development.
  • Recharts: Interactive data visualisations.
  • Antigravity: AI-assisted development workflow.

Mention only the tools your team actually used in the final implementation.

5. Use of Super Intelligence (50 words)

We use AI-assisted development and machine learning concepts to support data exploration and identify patterns in microgravity combustion data. These capabilities can help simplify complex scientific information, generate visual insights and support researchers in investigating flame behaviour. AI supports the analysis; it does not replace scientific validation or human judgement.

6. How is your project creative?

Our creativity lies in combining space science, artificial intelligence and interactive data visualisation into one platform. Instead of presenting raw combustion data, we aim to transform it into understandable visual insights. The space-themed interface and analytical approach make complex microgravity research more accessible to a wider audience.

7. What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered:

  • Scientific accuracy and reliability of NASA data.
  • Availability and quality of experimental datasets.
  • Differences between normal-gravity and microgravity combustion.
  • Feasibility of applying machine learning techniques.
  • Ease of use and accessibility of the platform.
  • Limitations of the available data.
  • Potential contribution to future spacecraft fire-safety research.
